Here, we report an energy level engineered compact-porous NiOx ( cp -NiOx) layer fabricated by two step spin- and spray-coating techniques with an enhanced electron blocking effect and high transmittance for highly efficient ST-PSCs and TSCs. The compactNiOx ( c -NiOx) HTL can enable efficient and selective collection of charges from the perovskite layer. The spray-deposition of high crystalline NiOx colloidal particles led to a mesoporous film which can be used to control the crystallization of the perovskite material and increase the contact area between HTL/perovskite interface.

Next, we conducted a systematic study of the morphology and topological properties of the c -NiOx and cp -NiOx films. The surface morphologies of the c -NiOx and cp -NiOx HTLs over the ITO substrates are displayed in Figs. 3a and 3b. The c -NiOx film exhibited a compact morphology of small particulates with a film thickness of ∼ 20 nm (Fig. S10). A total optimized thickness of ∼ 35 nm was obtained after spray-coating of the NiOx colloidal suspension over the ∼ 20 nm thick c -NiOx film. The morphology of the cp -NiOx film had a relatively loose texture and mesoporous morphology in comparison to its highly compact counterpart.

Here, we report an energy level engineered compact-porous NiOx ( cp -NiOx) layer fabricated by two step spin- and spray-coating techniques with an enhanced electron blocking effect and high transmittance for highly efficient ST-PSCs and TSCs. The compactNiOx ( c -NiOx) HTL can enable efficient and selective collection of charges from the perovskite layer. The spray-deposition of high crystalline NiOx colloidal particles led to a mesoporous film which can be used to control the crystallization of the perovskite material and increase the contact area between HTL/perovskite interface.

Next, we conducted a systematic study of the morphology and topological properties of the c -NiOx and cp -NiOx films. The surface morphologies of the c -NiOx and cp -NiOx HTLs over the ITO substrates are displayed in Figs. 3a and 3b. The c -NiOx film exhibited a compact morphology of small particulates with a film thickness of ∼ 20 nm (Fig. S10). A total optimized thickness of ∼ 35 nm was obtained after spray-coating of the NiOx colloidal suspension over the ∼ 20 nm thick c -NiOx film. The morphology of the cp -NiOx film had a relatively loose texture and mesoporous morphology in comparison to its highly compact counterpart.

This work demonstrated the fabrication of a dopant-free, highly transparent compact-porous-NiOx HTL for applications in ST-PSCs and perovskite/silicon TSCs. The cp -NiOx HTL was sequentially fab­ ricated by sol-gel and spray deposition techniques using NiOx pre­ cursor salt and highly crystalline NiOx colloidal particles, respectively. The cp -NiOx film demonstrated a mesoporous and pinhole-free morphology, enhanced transmittance, better energy band alignment with perovskite layer, and control over the formation of the perovskite films. The device performance of ST-PSCs based on cp -NiOx HTL was investigated taking compact-NiOx HTL as a reference.

Here, we report an energy level engineered compact-porous NiOx ( cp -NiOx) layer fabricated by two step spin- and spray-coating techniques with an enhanced electron blocking effect and high transmittance for highly efficient ST-PSCs and TSCs. The compactNiOx ( c -NiOx) HTL can enable efficient and selective collection of charges from the perovskite layer. unresolved_notes: The source reports both a precursor composition, Cs0.25FA0.75PbI2.4Br0.6, and a Results-section composition used in this work, Cs0.25FA0.75PbI0.8Br0.2. Both are preserved without attempting to reconcile or rewrite them.

The source reports family-level average transmittance values of ∼ 86 % and ∼ 92 % over 800-1200 nm for c-NiOx and cp-NiOx ST-PSCs, respectively (span-7757653b5832). These values are not assigned to the Table 1 individual devices because the evidence does not identify the measured physical specimens, and the schema has no family-level generic property field.

Table S6 reports 92.2 (800-1200) together with the exact cp-NiOx ST-PSC performance values, but its shorthand structure, “FTO/ NiO x / CsFAPbI 3 /PC 6 0 BM/ZnO/ITO/MgF 2,” conflicts with the main-text ITO/cp-NiOx/Cs-FA iodide-bromide/PC60BM/ZnO NPs/a-ITO description. The transmittance is retained on the coordinated Table S6 device result, but the conflicting shorthand stack is not used to redefine a family.

The p-NiOx ST-PSC is explicitly described as a best ST-PSC with ∼ 14 % performance, but the evidence does not establish its complete stack or whether all non-HTL layers are shared with the c-NiOx and cp-NiOx designs. It therefore remains an individual device with no assigned family.

The EQE-integrated-current passage identifies c-NiOx- and cp-NiOx-based PSC devices but does not establish whether they are the Table 1 ST-PSCs, the opaque devices, or other physical specimens. Separate devices with unknown family links are retained.

The main text reports a cp-NiOx opaque-device hysteresis index of 0.059, whereas Table S1 reports 0.093 for both reverse- and forward-scan rows. Both source-reported values are preserved without selecting one.
The complete functional-layer stack of the crystalline SiSC bottom cell is not reported. Only its crystalline-silicon absorber identity and reported size are represented.
The source states that the SiSC and ST-PSC J-V and EQE measurements were conducted separately. Tandem PCE observations are therefore not merged with the separate subcell observations.

The ∼ 500 nm perovskite-film statement in the tandem discussion is associated with demonstrating the cp-NiOx ST-PSC optical filter. It is retained for the cp-NiOx tandem top cell and is not propagated to the c-NiOx tandem without explicit support.

The water-droplet tests used PSC specimens with and without an a-ITO electrode for water-resistance characterization, not reported photovoltaic aging outcomes, so they are excluded from StabilityTest records.
Film-only, interface, TRPL, SCLC hole-only, and other partial-stack characterization specimens are excluded as photovoltaic device families.

The EIS recombination resistances (≈ 105 Ω and ≈ 243 Ω) are reported for c-NiOx- and cp-NiOx-based PSCs, but the supplied evidence does not identify the complete architecture or an individual physical device to which these measurements can be safely linked.
Spray-cycle optimization is a fabrication-parameter arm and does not create additional device families; the reported optimum of ∼ 6 spray cycles is retained in cp-NiOx processing conditions.
Table S1 reports a hysteresis index of 0.093 for the cp-NiOx device, whereas the main text reports 0.059; both source-reported values are retained without choosing between them.
The EIS passage identifies c-NiOx- and cp-NiOx-based PSCs but does not establish whether they are opaque or semitransparent devices, so the EIS specimens are not linked to an existing device family.

The supplied evidence supports replacing the separate Ar and O2 flow-rate values in fam-st-c and fam-st-cp with the coordinated source value “40:0.2 sccm,” but complete safe family replacements cannot be emitted without reproducing the otherwise unchanged full records.

The cited evidence for fam-tandem-c describes the c-NiOx film as exhibiting a “compact morphology of small particulates,” not the current material_form_raw value “compact morphology”; a complete family replacement is not emitted because the remainder of that large record is unchanged.
